A1.justification: Both PDFs describe GameDevBench and provide readable main text, tables, figures, and appendices. The retained sections and appendices can be matched despite substantial reformatting and additional evaluations in v2.

before.justification: v1 reports original evaluations on 132 game-development tasks, including agent success rates, feedback ablations, cost comparisons, and failure analysis.

after.justification: v2 reports original evaluations on 333 tasks and additional core/full, difficulty, failure-pattern, and transcript-contamination results in Appendices H–J.

M1.justification: The task-construction pipeline, deterministic Godot testing, screenshot MCP, and runtime-video feedback mechanisms remain unchanged. Appendices A–D contain identical construction, refinement, annotation, and agent prompts apart from formatting. Difficulty labeling extends evaluation rather than changing the proposed solving method.

E1.justification: The main benchmark retains Godot 4 and the same four development skill categories; its larger task count does not establish a new development domain. Appendix J adds a distinct evaluation task: completing held-out tutorial transcripts to probe memorization.

E2.justification: Table 2 substantially revises the evaluated lineup: GPT-5.4 and GPT-5.4 Mini replace GPT-5.1-Codex-Max, Qwen3.5-397B replaces Qwen3-VL-235B, and Claude Opus 4.5 is removed. The OpenHands comparison also removes Claude Sonnet 4.5 while retaining Haiku 4.5, Gemini 3 Flash, and Kimi K2.5.

E3.justification: The evaluation changes from 115 base tasks plus 17 variants to 154 core tasks plus 179 variants. v2 adds core/full reporting and a human-labeled split of 131 easy and 202 hard tasks. New protocols include LLM classification of failures from four leading configurations and first-half-to-second-half continuation of 117 transcripts, scored with ROUGE-L and BLEU-4. The main pass@1 metric remains unchanged.

E4.justification: Appendix H adds analyses of variant inclusion and human-rated multimodal difficulty; Appendix I supplements the existing qualitative failure discussion with quantified error categories; Appendix J adds a memorization probe. Feedback ablations are also revised: for example, Sonnet 4.5 loses its screenshot-only and video-only evaluations, while GPT-5.4 Mini receives both.

E5.justification: v1 Figure 6 reports a linear fit used to contextualize cost versus success; v2 removes that fitted statistical summary. Neither version reports repeated-run variability, seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests. Appendix F retains the same mean, three-standard-deviation-filtered mean, median, and maximum reporting convention.

E6.justification: Results are extensively replaced and supplemented. With both feedback tools, Table 2 reports Gemini 3 Pro at 54.5% in v1 versus 53.8% in v2, and Sonnet 4.5 at 46.2% versus 34.8%; these use different task sets and are not same-setting performance declines. Tables 4–8 add subgroup scores, token and cost values, failure frequencies, and transcript-overlap scores. Task statistics also change. Appendix G's new GPT-5.4 attribution is uncertain because Figure 11 still labels the example GPT-Codex-5.1-Max.

T1.justification: Neither version develops formal theoretical results, proofs, or substantive mathematical derivations. The added empirical metrics and subgroup comparisons do not introduce new mathematical theory.

C1.justification: The central claims remain a first benchmark for agentic game development, deterministic verification of multimodal tasks, persistent weaknesses in multimodal understanding, and benefits from visual feedback. Updated task counts, models, and performance examples change the supporting evidence without redefining these central contributions.

C2.justification: v2 drops v1's hypothesis that dynamically choosing between feedback mechanisms explains improved cost efficiency. It newly attributes lower full-set performance to multimodal variants, hypothesizes that Gemini 3 Pro's difficulty-split exception reflects stronger multimodal understanding, and interprets low transcript overlap as suggesting no systemic memorization. The new Impact Statement also explicitly bounds the tasks to using existing assets rather than creating assets.

D1.justification: v2 documents the new diagnostic procedures and supplies per-configuration median token consumption and costs in Table 4. It removes v1 Figure 6's disclosure that Gemini CLI costs were approximated using OpenHands, without explaining whether cost collection changed. Exact prompts in Appendices A–D and the public repository remain unchanged; the failure judge's identity and prompt are unspecified.

R1.justification: v2 replaces the SlideChat pathology-image reference with SlideGen for the slide-generation comparison and adds BenchLM.ai as a source for the Design2Code comparison. The broader positioning relative to software benchmarks, computer-use agents, game playing, and specialized game-development systems remains substantially unchanged.

P1.justification: The main section sequence and Appendices A–G are retained. v2 locally rewrites the abstract, results discussion, and conclusion, changes 'framework' terminology to 'harness,' adopts author–year citations, and adds acknowledgements, an Impact Statement, and Appendices H–J. Most construction, method, related-work, and prompt text remains closely matched.

P2.justification: v2 changes the main text to a two-column conference layout with running headers, resizes and relocates existing displays, stacks Figure 5's panels, and substantially redraws Figure 6 with model-family groupings and harness encodings. It adds Tables 4–8. The task-example figures and Figure 11's underlying graphic are retained rather than newly introduced.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the benchmark's empirical validation beyond v1's category-level comparisons and illustrative failure case. Core/full and easy/hard analyses directly examine the intended multimodal challenge, quantified failure categories improve diagnostic value, and the transcript probe adds a limited contamination check. These address substantive validation gaps rather than merely increasing task counts. The unspecified failure judge and contradictory model attribution in Figure 11 limit reproducibility and consistency, but do not outweigh the added evidence.
